ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Operation to flush out ultras in J&K 
*141. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether security forces in Jammu and Kashmir have launched a drive 
to flush out ultras from mountain hide-outs in J&K; and 
(b) if so, the number of ultras captured or killed in the operation and the 
arms and ammunition seized from their hide-outs, and the number of Indian 
security personnel who laid down their lives during the operation? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Counter terrorist operations are carried out regularly in the 
State of Jammu & Kashmir, including remote hilly areas for flushing out 
terrorists. 
One of such operations named 'Operation Sarp Vinash' carried out 
recently, has resulted in the killing of 65 terrorists, arrest of 3 terrorists, 
capture of 79 pieces of major weapons and large quantities of war like stores. 
During this Operation, 5 Army personnel laid down their lives.

SHRI N. JOTHI: Hon. Chairman, Sir, we have been facing this problem 
of cross-border terrorism for the last ten years, by whatever name one may 
call it, whether it is 'proxy war' — the phrase used quite often by hon. Deputy 
Prime Minister — or the problem of 'ultras' or 'insurgents' or whatever. You 
need not tell me about your blueprint. Le t it be an Army secret. But does this 
Government have any idea of how to pu t an end to the entire issue of cross-
border terrorism in Kashmir so that our yatris do not get killed, or our jawans 
do not get ambushed, and the people of that State can also  live as peacefully 
as the people of any other State? Has the Government got any programme in 
this regard? If it is an Army secret, you  need not tell us about it. However, I 
would like to know whether there was any time-bound programme on this. 
What is the point in keeping the barracks full of Army there not doing 
anything to tackle the situation, and letting our innocent citizens be killed? We 
keep getting anguished over this matter every moment we read about this. 
What is the programme of the Government in this regard?

any attack on innocent citizens or on the troops is something, which is 
common to all of us. In so far as the hon. Member's question as to what 
exactly is being done in Kashmir, well,  there is nothing secret about the 
operations that are going on and these operations are taking care of the 
enemy attacks. But there are situations where the fidayeen move in, and there 
is no way that anyone can identify a fidayeen team or an individual as and 
when he approaches. And many of th e killings that take place in Jammu & 
Kashmir are essentially fidayeen attacks and one has to  face them; and the 
army is well-equipped to face them.

Statement 
(a) The State Government of J&K have in formed that a total of 1,11,932 
Yatris have registered for Amarnath Yatra this year. However, the number of 
persons who could have Darshan would depend on various factors like 
weather/climatic conditions, security threat, etc. 
(b) It is the responsibility of the State Government of J&K to provide 
security and make all other arrangements for the Amarnath Yatra. Central Police 
Forces are deployed in J&K as an aid to the State Government, keeping in view 
the overall security scenario and availability of these Forces. Like every year, 
additional forces have been provided to the Government of J&K to make security 
arrangements for the Amarnath Yatra 2003. 
The State Government have info rmed that elaborate security 
arrangements have been made for Amarnath Yatra at the base camp, along the 
track as well as at the Holy Cave. As  regards catering facilities, the State 
Government has issued necessary license s for operating lungars at different 
places along the track. 
(c) The expenditure on the Amarnath Yatra is borne by the State 
Government of J&K. However, Government of India is only assisting the 
State Government of J&K through deployment of additional Security Forces. 
The State Government has constituted an Amarnath Yatra Shrine Board for the 
smooth conduct of the Yatra. 
(d) The number of Yatris registered this year is slightly higher than the 
actual visited during Amarnath Yatra 2002, which was 1,10,793.

during April-June, 2003, as ascertained from Gujarat Electricity Board was of 
the order of 12.7% and peaking shortage 18.7%. 
30 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) The shortage is mainly on account of growth in demand outstripping 
the growth in generation and generation capacity addition. 
(c) According to Gujarat Electricity Board, the total availability as on 
30th June, 2003 was 6060 MW as against a demand of 6290 MW 
representing a shortage of 230 MW. 
(d) Supply and distribution of electricity is the responsibility of the State 
Government. Electricity, being a concurrent subject, Government of India 
supplements the efforts of State Government by setting up power plants in 
Central Sector through Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs. Gujarat 
has a firm allocation of 1538 MW in Central Generating Stations (CGS) in 
Western Region (WR. In addition, the following steps have been/being taken in 
order to mitigate power shortage in Gujarat:—  
(i) Gujarat has been allocated 164 MW from unallocated quota of CGS 
in WR and 80 MW from unallocated quota of NTPC stations in Eastern 
Region (ER. 
(ii) Besides capacity addition of 431  MW in State Sector and 500 MW 
in Private Sector in Gujarat, generation capacity of 5367 MW in 
Central Sector in Western Region and 1450 MW multi-state project 
(Sardar Sarovar Hydro Project) is planned to be set up during 10th 
Plan in which Gujarat will have entitlements. 
(iii) Implementation of Renovation, Modernization and Life Extension 
(R&M & LE) Schemes for old and inefficient generating units for 
overall improvement in generation performance. 
(iv) Demand Side Management, promotion of energy efficiency and 
energy conservation measures. 
(v) Enhancement in evacuation of surplus power from Eastern Region to 
other regions by setting up of inter-regional links. With the 
commissioning of 400 KV Rourkela-Raipur double circuit 
transmission line, the two regional grids viz. Eastern and Western 
Grids have been connected in synchronous mode. Gujarat is also a 
beneficiary of ER power.

Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) which is intended 
for up-gradation of sub-transmission and distribution in densely 
electrified zones in the urban a nd industrial areas and improvement 
in commercial viability of State Electricity Boards by reducing the 
aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses. During the year

Gold Wealth Beneath Deccan Plateau 
*155.  MISS MABEL REBELLO: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that vast untapped gold wealth lies beneath 
Deccan plateau and it is proposed to exploit these dormant untapped 
potentials; 
(b) the progress made in mining of Huti region gold mines in Karnataka 
and other similarly placed mines in the country; and 
(c) the reasons for lagging behind Australia in gold mining when both 
the countries have similar geographical characteristics such as rock formation 
and the soil beneath surface? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF MINES (SHRI 
RAMESH BAIS): (a) As per Geological Survey of India (GSI), a subordinate 
office under the Ministry of Mines, the geological set up below the Deccan 
Plateau does not suggest occurrence of vast untapped gold wealth. 
(b) In Hutti region, Karnataka, Hutti Gold Mines Limited (HGML), a 
Government of Karnataka Undertaking, operates two units i.e. (i) The 
Hutti Gold Unit (HGU) - comprising Hutti Gold Mines (under ground), 
Uti (Open-cast Mines) and Hirab-Buddini (Exploratory mine), in Raichur 
District and (ii) Chitradurga Gold Unit (CGU) - comprising Ajjanahalli 
(open-cast mine) in Tumkur District and G.R. Halli (exploratory 
underground mine) in Chitradurga District. During the year 2002-2003, 
HGML produced 2709 kgs. of Gold. 
The other gold mines of Bharat Gold Mines Limited (BGML) in the 
Kolar Gold Fields of Karnataka and in Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh have 
been closed due to uneconomic operations. 
(c) Even though there is similarity in the geological setup, structure, 
tectonics and metaliogeny between Yilgarn and Pilbara cartons of 
Australia and Dharwar Craton of Peninsular India, the extent of 
mineralization can vary from craton to  craton. In India the mining has 
been limited to a few relatively high tenor deposits of a minimum 3 g/ 
tonne of primary gold. The occurrences are few and wide apart. In 
40 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Australia the number of reported gold occurrences is much more and both 
underground and opencast mechanized mining is practiced. 
Studies on Abnormal Increase in Summer Temperature 
*156. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the disaster management wing of Home Ministry is aware 
of the fact that several parts of the country, mainly Andhra Pradesh, 
recorded unprecedented high temperature in the summer of 2003; 
(b) whether any agency studies the reas ons for the abnormal increase in 
the average summer temperature in the States like Andhra Pradesh; 
(c) if so, the findings thereof; 
(d) if not, whether Government intend to ask any of our scientific 
agencies to find the scientific reasons for the unusual phenomenon; and 
(e) the action plan to save the poor people from calamity of heat wave 
during summer? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SWAMI CHINMAYANAND): (a) During 2003, heat wave conditions in 
Andhra Pradesh prevailed for a duration of 27 days from 16th May to 11th 
June, whereas in normal cases, it lasts only for about a week or so. Regions 
extending from Rajasthan to coastal Orissa and Andhra Pradesh across 
Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra are prone to heat waves. Its occurrence year 
after year varies in space and time from one region to another. 
(b) and (c) According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), this 
year a cyclonic storm development over the Bay of Bengal and remained over 
the sea for about 10 days (10-19 May. It had a prolonged influence on the flow 
pattern over the country even after its dissipation. This caused the dry and hot 
northwesterly winds to blow over the peninsula leading to heat wave 
conditions over Andhra Pradesh and its prevalence for an unusualy longer 
duration. Pre-Monsoon showers during summer generally bring respite from 
rising maximum temperatures and consequent improvement in heat wave 
conditions. But this year the 
41 

RAJYA  SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
absence of such rainfall activity significantly contributed to the severity of 
heat wave conditions in Andhra Pradesh. The delay in the onset of the 
monsoon this year also favoured the continuance of heat wave conditions for 
a longer period in June. 
The impact of the heat wave conditions  was also felt rather acutely this 
year due to the prevalence of drought conditions in some regions because of 
poor monsoon rains last year. 
(d) The State Governments concerned take necessary steps to mitigate 
the impact of this problem.

generation/power purchase costs ar e the key measures necessary to

Bagga Committee Report 
1057. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state:

Progression, for army officers and to ex amine a proposal fo r restructuring of

(c) the time by which this report is likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) to 
(c) A Committee was set up under the Chairmanship of the Special Secretary, 
Ministry of Defence on 16th July, 2001 to exmine Army Headquarters 
proposal for the re-structuring of the officers' cadre of the Army. The 
Committee identified two inter-related i ssues at the core of the structural 
imbalances referred to by the Army Headquarters i.e. high age profile and cadre 
stagnation. In order to achieve the objective of bringing down the age profile

tenures outside the Army, exit through voluntary severance scheme and

support cadre more attractive, have been recommended to be worked out 
pragmatically.

issues, no specific time-frame for implementation can be indicated.

State Governments for calamity management throughout the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SWAMI CHINMAYANAND): (a) India has been highly vulnerable to

have not carried out an assessment of the losses suffered by the State on 
account of all types of natural calam ities. However, natural calamities

Protection to Indian Garment Exporters in WTO 
1170. SHRI G.K. VASAN: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government propose to take steps to protect the interest of 
Indian garments exporters in WTO; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
BASANAGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Government have been 
taking appropriate steps to protect the interests of Indian textiles export industry 
including garments in the WTO. Some of the recent steps taken are given 
below:- 
170 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(i) India has raised a dispute under the Dispute Settlement Mechanism of 
WTO challenging the zero cutoms duty concession accorded by European 
Communities to the ready-made garments and made-up articles originating 
from some of our competing countries under the special tariff arrangements to 
combat drug production and trafficking of its new GSP Scheme, which are 
perceived by India to cause adverse trade effects on our industry. 
(ii) The United States had on 31st January 2003 requested WTO's 
Committee on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures that the export 
competitiveness of textile and apparel exports from India be determined on the 
basis of a computation undertaken by  the WTO Secretariat in accordance 
with Article 27.6(b) of the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing 
Measures. The products for which the request was made included all tex tiles 
and apparel products under Harmonized System Nomenclature chapters 50-
59 and 60-63. India has sought certain clarifications from the WTO 
Secretariat in this regard. 
(iii) India along with the certain members of International Textiles & 
Clothing Bureau (ITCB) made a submission in the WTO General Council for 
availability of flexibility of 'Carry-Forward' of quotas in the year 2004. 
(iv) India along with other ITCB members raised the issue inter-alia of 
advancing the application of the higher "growth-on-growth" factor of 27% 
w.e.f. 1st January 2000, which was otherwise under the Agreement on Textiles & 
Clothing (ATC) to be applied on 1st January 2002. However, no recommendations 
could be forwarded by the Council for Trade in Goods to the General 
Council in this regard.

Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state:

2003) have been Rs. 2400.76 crore as compared to Rs. 1894.83 crore of the 
corresponding period of the previous year. Thus, the handloom exports, in 
general, have shown a growth of 26.70% during 2002-03. 
(c) Does not arise. However, in general, the following steps have been

the Handloom Export Promotion Council;

promotion schemes such as Duty Entitlement Pass Book Scheme/Duty 
Drawback Scheme etc; 
(g) Technology Upgradation Fund to upgrade technology; 
(h) Supply of Hank Yarn at Mill Gate prices through the National 
Handloom Development Corporation; 
(i) Financial assistance provided under the Handloom Export Scheme for 
development of exportable products and publicity & marketing thereof; 
(j) Updating of website at frequent intervals to update information to the 
buyers about the handloom products; and

Cauvery and Krishna rivers and action taken by Government with regard

SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I beg to call the attention 
of the Minister of Water Resources to the situation arising out of disputes over 
the sharing of inter-state river waters of Cauvery and Krishna rivers and 
action taken by Government with regard thereto. 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI) : Sir, the dispute relating to sharing of Cauvery water among States of 
Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Pondicherry was referred to the Cauvery 
Water Disputes Tribunal (CWDT) constituted on June 2, 1990. The Tribunal has 
not submitted its final report and decision. 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
The CWDT had in June, 1991, passed an interim order directing the 
State of Karnataka for releasing water fr om its reservoirs so as to ensure 205 
thousand million cubic ft. (TMC) of water in Mettur reservoir of Tamil Nadu in 
a water year, in fixed monthly and weekly pattern. The Tribunal had also given 
certain clarifications in April, 1992 and December, 1995, on its Order of June, 
1991. 
The Central Government had published the Order of the Tribunal 
under section 6 of the Inter State Wa ter Disputes (ISWD) Act, 1956 in 1991, 
thus, making the Order final and binding on the parties to the dispute. The 
Order of the Tribunal is to be given effect to by the party States. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI NILOTPAL BASU) in the Chair] 
Further, under the provisions of section 6 A of the ISWD Act, 1956, 
the Central Government has notif ied a Scheme called Cauvery Water 
(implementation of the Or der of 1991 and all subsequent Related Orders of 
the Tribunal) Scheme, 1998, consisting  of Cauvery River Authority and 
Monitoring Committee. The Cauvery Rive r Authority consists of the Prime 
Minister as Chairperson and Chief Minist ers of the basin States as members. 
The authority has held six meetings so far, and the Monitoring Committee has 
held 17 meetings. 
Sir, regarding Krishna Water Dispu tes, the Central Government 
constituted the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (KWDT) in April, 1969, for 
adjudication of the water disputes of  Krishna. The Krishna Water Disputes 
Tribunal submitted its report and decision in 1976. The decision was published 
by Central Government in the Official Gazette on 31.5.1976. As per the KWDT 
direction, at any time after 31 st May, 2000, the order of the KWDT may be 
reviewed or revised by a competent authority or Tribunal. 
The Central Government received requests under Section 3 of the 
Inter-State River Water Disputes (ISRWD) Act, 1956, from the States of 
Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pr adesh in October, 2002, December, 
2002 and January, 2003 respectively requesting for constitution of a Krishna 
Water Disputes Tribunal under section 4 of the ISRWD Act, 1956, and 
referring to the tribunal for adjudication and decision, the water disputes and 
matters connected therewith or relevant to water disputes emerging from the 
letters of complaint.   The constitution of a second Tribunal for Krishna

SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nomin ated): Madam, the essence of 
the Cauvery dispute is a c onflict of interests between Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, 
Kerala, and Pondicherry. Any fair sharing would have to provide for the 
legitimate interests of all the four parties. The time has come to rise above 
narrow political considerations and arrive at a settlement that ensures justice to 
all the aggrieved parties. Rainfall dist ribution over short periods in the 
catchment area of a river is a fact or that comes up when assessing the 
quantity of river-water needed for surface irrigation. Over short periods, the 
rainfall situation in catchment areas and in the basin of the river will vary from 
year to year. Thus, arrangements of water distribution and/or sharing made on 
the basis of averages wi ll not often work in real time. Near continuous 
monitoring of rainfall in all years, t herefore, becomes esse ntial. This means 
that technical experts as well as representatives of farmers'

organizations in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Pondicherry should be 
included in CRA. Is the Government considering expansion of the Cauvery 
Regulatory Authority (CRA)? During floods, Tamil Nadu will be used as a 
drainage area by Karnataka. Such flood water overflows cannot be used in a 
planned manner. Thus, any arbitrating authority on the sharing of Cauvery 
waters should not only indicate the quantum of water to be supplied by 
Karnataka to Tamil Nadu, but also specify the period and intervals over which 
such deliveries are to be effected. Unfo rtunately, the Governments of the two 
principal contending States  have, over the years,  generated and fostered 
strong sentiments among the general public, which tend to limit their own 
negotiating freedom and flexibility. The Cauvery is a fabled river with strong 
historical, religious and cultural asso ciations in both Karnataka and Tamil 
Nadu. In both States, all parties tend to take a strong stand on this issue, 
making it risky for whichever party is in power to give the impression of being 
weak or failing to project the interests of the State. That is why this dispute has 
become so intractable. According to late  Shri S. Guhan, an administrator and 
academician who authored the Cauvery River Dispute which represented an 
authoritative and scholarly track on the Cauvery issue, and I quote, "A 
settlement of the Cauvery di spute, if it is to be settled in the long term, will 
require two conditions to be met. First, it must be fair and equitable to all the 
basin States and perceived as such by them. Secondly, it is necessary 
politically to create a spirit of goodwill and cooperation during the process of 
arriving at a settlement, and to sustain it thereafter when the agreement begins 
to be implemented. What effort has the Central Government made to create 
this climate of goodwill between the contentious parties? Given the uncertainty 
of water release, the cultivation of the Kuruvai crop in Tamil Nadu will be risky 
in most years. Farmers here must be weaned away from the concept of the 
Kuruvai crop as a non-negotiable one. Perhaps, the time has come to demand 
a national crop pattern policy. So, in drought-hit Marathwada, farmers are 
dissuaded from growing sugarcane, and, in the water-scarce Cauvery delta, 
farmers are dissuaded from producing paddy, both water-guzzling crops. Has 
the Government considered putting into place this National Crop Pattern 
Policy? From the point of view of assured water availability, the cropping 
season of rice in the deltaic areas of  Tamil Nadu can only be for eight months 
from August to March. Even this period cannot continuously be used for rice 
because of intervening cloudy and wet weather months from mid October to 
mid December. So,' we can have a rice crop from the beginning of September  
to   mid-January,   preceded  and  followed   by  suitable   short-

duration crops. The machinery for resolvi ng the water disputes is not written 
into the Corporation Laws, but has been provided for by Parliament in the 
Inter-State Disputes Act, 1956. This Act empowers the Central Government to 
constitute adjudication tribunals on inter-State water disputes, and in ensuring 
the implementations of the decisions of  the Tribunal. But Section II of the Act 
excludes the jurisdiction of all courts in respect of any inter-State water dispute 
referred to a tribunal. Does this include the Supreme Court also? There are 
some grey judicial areas in inter-State water disputes that need to be sorted

to this conclusion not on the merits of the case, but because it had no 
jurisdiction on the matter. Consequently, referring this issue to a new Tribunal

this could be done by suitable legislat ion. The Chief Minister of Andhra 
Pradesh has written to the Centre to ta ke necessary action under Section 66A 
of the Andhra State Act, 1953. What is the Government doing in this regard?

THE MERCHANT SHIPPING (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2003 
THE  MINISTER  OF SHIPPING  (SHRI  SHATRUGHAN  SINHA):     I 
move : 
"That the Bill further to amend the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, be 
taken into consideration." 
259 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
With your permission, I would like to say a few words about the 
Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2003. 
India is an active and prominent member of the International 
Maritime Organisation (IMO), the spec ialised U.N. body responsible for 
establishing and enforcing world standards  in maritime shipping. We enjoy a 
high reputation as a leading maritime country and as a major supplier of 
officers to the world maritime industry. 
Apart from the image that India carries as a world class maritime 
country strictly adhering to international norms end regulations, it also has 
international obligation to continuously upgrade the quality of its shipping. 
Laws pertaining to shipping and maritime affairs have global relevance. Our 
ships have to trade internationally and could be subjected to inspections at 
foreign ports to check their compliance with IMO Conventions and protocols 
whose status keeps changing. Similarly, foreign flagships will also be 
subjected to inspections when they visit Indian ports with a view to protecting 
our waters from environmental hazards. In order to implement the conventions 
and protocols to which India has become a party and to be in line with 
international standards, India is required to incorporate the provisions of these 
conventions and protocols in our merchant shipping legislation. We have to be 
dynamic and responsive to both need and time, and the present effort is to 
incorporate the provisions of the c onventions and protocols acceded to by 
India in the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. Once the proposed amendments 
are approved by Parliament, India will be able to keep up with its international 
obligations. 
The International Maritime Organisation adopted in 1973 the 
International Convention for Prevention  of Pollution from Ships, 1973 
(MARPOL 1973), which was amended by adoption of Protocol in 1978. The 
MARPOL 1973 and Protocol of 1978 thereto, together known as MARPOL 
73/78 seeks to achieve complete elimination of pollution of the marine 
environment by oil and other harmful substances and minimization of 
accidental discharge of such substances by prescribing a package of 
requirements of design, construction, survey and other certification norms with 
respect to discharge of sewage and garbage into the sea. 
MARPOL 73/78 has six Annexes specifying the technical 
requirements to be complied by ships for the purpose of safety of life at sea 
260 

[30 July, 20031 RAJYA SABHA 
as well as prevention of pollution from ships. In accordance with Article 14 of 
the MARPOL 1973 and Article II of its 1978 Protocol, the provisions of 
Annexes I and II are mandatory for contra cting States while implementation of 
Annexes III, IV and V was optional. In dia acceded to MARPOL 1973, as 
modified by its Protocol of 1978 alo ng with Annexes I and II, by depositing the 
Instrument of Accession with IMO on 24th September, 1986. The instrument of 
accession deposited by India contained a declaration "that the Government of 
the Republic of India shall not be bound by the provisions of Annexes III, IV 
and V of the said Convention." It was decided not to accede to these annexes 
because by that time, major maritime States had not acceded to these three 
optional annexes: It was decided to firs t understand the imp lications of the 
provisions contained in these annexes. As a number of countries have since 
acceded to these annexes, India has also acceded to these three annexes to 
ensure that Indian ships are not targeted for non-compliance while visiting the 
ports of such countries. Also, accession to these annexes would enable Indian 
to take steps as per the convention to prevent pollution in India waters. 
-Article 15(2) of the Convention, as amended by the Protocol of 1978, 
stipulates that the optiona l annexes shall enter into force internationally, 
twelve months after the date on which not less than 15 States, the combined 
merchant fleets of which constitute not less than fifty per cent of gross 
tonnage of world's merchant ships, have become parties to it. As on 30 th 
November, 2002, the Annexes III, IV and V have been ratified or acceded to 
by 105, 89 and 110 States respec tively. The percentages of combined 
merchant fleet belonging to these Stat es who have become parties to these 
optional Annexes are 82.95, 51.14 and 89.26, respectively. Annexure III and 
Annexure V have come into force inte rnationally on 1.7.1992 and 31.12.1988 
respectively. Annexure IV will come into force on 27.9.2003. 
The main advantage arising from ratifying these Annexes is that the 
Indian as well as foreign vessels plying on overseas trade world-wide would 
automatically follow the universal st andards on the subject. Once these 
Annexes are acceded to, the reception facilities as contained in these 
Annexes are to be provided by the Ports where vessels call. This will, in turn, 
help us to develop service facilities in Indian Ports comparable to standards 
available elsewhere. 
261 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
[THE VICE CHAIRMAN (SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY) in the Chair] 
The system of prevention of pollu tion (i) by harmful substances 
carried by sea in packed forms and (ii) by sewage from ships, as well as the 
Waste and Garbage Management for disposal of garbage from ships in Port, 
etc. could be made mandatory so as  to ensure cleaner waters. Further, 
ratification of the Annexes under c onsideration may ensure avoiding any 
unreasonable application of strict Port State Control on Indian ships elsewhere 
in the world, thereby boosting the Indian maritime services. 
The Government of India has now decided to accede to the optional 
Annexures as the MARPOL 1973 and its Protocol of 1978 strengthened such 
anti pollution measures by introduci ng adequate design and constructional 
aspects of ships so as to control pollut ion of the sea by oil escaping into the 
sea, following marine casualties of t ankers. Besides, these two instruments 
are also intended to control pollution of the sea from: 
(a) harmful    substances    carried    in    package    forms,    freight 
containers, portable tankers and road or rail tank wagons; 
(b) noxious liquid substances in bulk; 
(c) sewage from ships; and 
(d) garbage from ships. 
To implement the provisions of the said Convention and the Protocol, 
the present Bill contains  amendments to 12 sections from section 356A to 
3560 under part XI A of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. 
Annexes I to V to MARPOL 73/78 contain many technical details and 
operational matters which often change with progress made in the sphere of 
technology, safety and environmental st andards. Therefore, it is not desirable 
to put such details in the body of t he Merchant Shipping Act since that would 
involve changing the Act frequently with th e changes in the provisions of the 
Annexes I to V of MARPOL 73/78. As su ch, it is proposed to amend sections 
356 E and 356 O to confer powers on the Central Government to make rules 
to prescribe these technical and operat ional requirements prescribed by the 
MARPOL 73/78 and its Annexes as amended from time to time.

With the proposed amendments, India will not only be able to meet 
its international commitments arising out of accession to Annexures III, IV and 
V to MARPOL 73/78 but also will be at par with the systems and requirements 
of other advanced maritime nations.

Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2003 for consideration by the House.

written in the Statement of Objects and R easons that as an active member of 
the International Maritime Organisation, India has acceded to a number of 
International Conventions and Protocols adopted by the IMO.    I think    it 
268 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
should not have been done so late. They have given more stress on issuing of 
certificates. But the question of vigi lance has been avoided. They have not 
given much importance to how pollution occurs and how it can be stopped. I 
understand that this Bill is in consonan ce with the international laws which 
were established as early as in 1954 in UK. What are the objectives of these 
laws? The objectives are: (a) prevention of willful attempt of pollution in the sea 
by oil; and (b) prevention from subst ances coming from offshore industries. 
But these things are not there in t he Bill. Then there is no mention of 
minimisation of spoilage of oil, pr evention of shore generated waste, air 
pollution and poisonous gases, in the Bill. Sir, oil pollution is of a great concern 
to us because oil comes from the Middl e-East. It comes across the seas. It 
cannot come by air as it will be very costly. It cannot come by road also. So, 
oil pollution is a very important thing which needs to be looked into. Sir, our 
coastal line is a very long line. Some Members say that it is 5,700 kms. of 
length. I think, it is more  than that. It will exceed 6,000 kms. Along the coastal 
line, there are as many as 50 cities, most ly industrial; small and big cities are 
there. And, many rivers have terminated into the seas. All these rivers carry 
huge quantity of untreated sewage and all these industrial cities discharge 
waste materials into the rivers and into the seas. All these things together 
pose a threat to our environment. The ecological balances are disturbed by 
this. Now. all these spoils have not got importance in this Bill. 
I would like to point but another important matter. In India, we are 
having the largest ship-breaking yard which is at Alang near Bhavnagar in 
Gujarat. What happens there? When t he lifetime of the ships exceed 25-30 
years, these are sent to Alang by the capitalists or by persons having special 
interests. There the ships are broken an d steel is taken from the body of the 
ships. About 70 per cent of the replaceable ships of the whole world come 
here. Substances like polychlorinated bi phenyls, zinc, lead, inflammable oil 
products, explosives, etc. are brought to Alang for breaking these ships, and 
by this, the pollution is intensified. Now, this aspect has not been considered 
in this Amendment Bill. 
Sir, the Amendment Bill has been brought in line with the 
international laws and as per the Convention of the IMO. Since we are a 
member of the IMO, we have to abide by it.. But the thing is that we have to 
be alert. If our sea-shores are not free from pollution, or, say, if we cannot 
have them up to the international level, a call may come to India to 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
sell the shores, and these may go in the hands of the imperialists. This type of 
occupation may take place because we are in this LPG (liberalisation, 
privatisation and globalisation) syst em. In the present situation when 
everything is being privatised, -- even the Airways are going to be privatised -- 
I am afraid, we are going into the domain of the imperialists. Hence care 
should be taken and every effort should be taken to prevent such a thing from 
happening. With these words, Sir, I conclude. Thank you.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Price Policy for Kharif Crops of 2003-2004 Season. 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI RAJNATH SINGH): Sir, 
the Government has fixed the Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for Fair 
Average Quality (FAQ) of Kharif Cr ops of 2003-2004 season. The MSP of 
paddy common and paddy Grade-A has been raised by Rs. 20 each as 
compared to the previous year and fixed at Rs. 550 and Rs. 580 per quintal 
respectively. 
The MSPs of Jowar, Bajra, Maize and Ragi have been raised by Rs. 
20 each and fixed at Rs. 505 per quintal as against Rs. 485 per quintal fixed 
for the previous year. 
The MSP of Arhar (Tur) has been raised to Rs. 1360 per quintal as 
against Rs. 1320 per quintal for the previous year, thus marking an increase 
of Rs. 40 per quintal. Similarly, the MSPs of Moong and Urad have been 
raised by "Rs. 40 per quintal as compared to the previous year. The Minimum 
Support Price of groundnut-in-shell has been fixed at Rs. 1400 per quintal 
marking an increase of Rs.-45-per Quinta l as compared to the last year.   
Similarly, the MSPs of soyabean (yellow) and soyabean (black) have 
281 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
been raised by Rs.45 per quintal and fixed at Rs.930 and Rs.840 per quintal 
respectively. 
The MSP of sunflower seed has  been raised from Rs.1195 per 
quintal last year to Rs.1250 per quintal for the 2003-04 season, marking an 
increase of Rs.55 per quintal. 
As compared to the last year, the MSPs of sesamum and Nigerseed 
have been fixed at Rs. 1485 per quintal and Rs.1155 per quintal respectively 
marking an increase of Rs.35 per quintal. 
The MSP of cotton (F-414/H-777/J-34) and (H-4) varieties have been 
raised by Rs.50 per quintal as compared to the previous year. 
It is expected that the increases e ffected in the MSPs of the kharif 
crops will encourage the farmers for increasing the production and productivity 
of the crops in the country and will also encourage the farmers in 
diversification of crops.
